hints.hint: To back anyone's "I cannot tell", exhibit TWO concrete scenarios agreeing on everything that person was told yet differing in the quantity at issue. Two named witnesses, not a vague count -- if you cannot name both, you credited someone with a fact the text never supplied. Watch for this: when the role of a given number is unsettled, each reading may on its own pin the value down, yet the person stays uncertain because the readings disagree on which value. Competing readings are themselves the source of ignorance, so a candidate that fails only after you fix one reading has not failed: keep it, and never call the problem broken. A later statement then demands that both of that speaker's witnesses survive what the earlier one revealed; chaining that is usually the solution. Use divisibility and bounds, not long lists. Check which quantity is asked, state your result before you run long, substitute back once, stop.
hints.mutation: replace vague 'intersect constraints across readings' with a constructive two-witness test for ignorance, and state that readings disagreeing on the pinned value is itself ignorance so a candidate refuted under one fixed reading survives
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent scored 0/8; 2 hit the 16384 cap and all eight burned 13k-16.4k tokens. Every rollout proved that under each fixed reading a speaker's own value pins the partner, declared both readings impossible, and then reported a factor or complement its own text had just refuted. One even reached the balanced split, said it forced knowledge, and reported a neighbour. So the binding error is not the ordering or the guessing ban but the criterion for ignorance itself: the student equates it with many partners inside one reading. I replaced the intersect-across-readings clause with a constructive test -- name two scenarios matching what the speaker was told but differing in the unknown -- and stated that two readings each pinning a DIFFERENT value already create ignorance, so a candidate refuted only under one fixed reading must be kept.

hints.hint:
When both sides have the same degree in the unknown, divide by one side so only a ratio survives and the relation collapses to w^n = c, pinning |w| exactly; here w=(z-1)/z. Invert the ratio to recover the unknown, convert the description into one exact equation in the coordinates, and complete the square to reach standard form and read off the requested parameter. Generally: normalize so the relation depends on a single quantity, and keep every value exact.

A check that disagrees with your derivation almost always means arithmetic inside the check, not a broken problem. Repair that one line only; never restart and never declare the setup inconsistent. Two exact points plus a symmetry axis pin a circle faster than a large linear system. State your simplified result as soon as you have one, then use leftover room to confirm it.
hints.mutation: restate the opening move as the general homogeneity/equal-degree trigger for dividing to a single ratio and w^n=c, keeping the incumbent's second paragraph intact

Rounds 5-16 all rewrote the second paragraph to bound, redirect or replace that audit loop, and all twelve lost transfer, so the loop language is not the lever. The untouched lever is the opening move, which since round 4 has read as a bare recipe for this equation. I keep the second paragraph verbatim and restate the first as its transferable trigger: equal degree on both sides licenses dividing to a single ratio, giving w^n = c and a pinned modulus.

hints.hint: Fix one setup and never rebuild it. Overlapping pieces obey total = sum minus overlap, so maximize coverage by minimizing overlap; the same bookkeeping serves counting. When a condition pins one piece by a corner, size never implies containment: only the angle at that corner limits its reach, so never argue from distances to a center - a corner is not a center. Turn the claim into arithmetic: write the two edges leaving the pinned corner as inequalities and test each vertex of the other piece against them. One vertex failing proves nothing is swallowed, so the overlap is a proper part and both extremes are wrong. Settle the free parameter by a trade, not by sampling: shift it slightly and compare what enters the overlap against what leaves. A match means it never mattered, so stop reasoning there. Open the visible reply with the arithmetic and your result; no headings, no restated setup, no closing re-test.
hints.mutation: make the non-containment check computational: test each vertex of the pinned piece against the two edge inequalities at the corner, instead of a qualitative wedge claim
hints.subagent_summary: Five of eight scored, so the sum-minus-overlap frame and trade test are kept. All three failures shared one error, not a budget problem: each asserted that the large piece's sides all sit at distance 1 from its center while the pinned piece only reaches 0.5, so containment holds at every rotation and the overlap equals the whole piece. One wrote that conclusion out confidently and stopped early with tokens to spare; the other two never closed reasoning, cycling 109-139 rotation retests around the same claim while repeatedly calling the geometry too complex to compute. The incumbent's qualitative wedge sentence and reference-point warning did not block it. This revision replaces them with a computational test: express the two edges leaving the pinned corner as inequalities and check each vertex of the other piece, so one failing vertex refutes containment numerically.

hints.hint:
For "at most how many" questions give both halves: a bound and an example reaching it. Name a count early, before you run long.

Never impose a constraint the problem did not state. Reuse is allowed unless forbidden, and a whole-pattern condition need not hold piece by piece. A branch ending in "impossible" or "unbounded" over-constrained something free; drop it, and do not retreat to the bare piece count.

Posit ONE unknown affine target for the whole pattern (an arithmetic progression is A+B*n) and ask where a piece agrees with it. A degree-d piece agrees at most d times, d exactly as given, not d-1 - that caps ONE piece, not the pattern. Agreement sets are disjoint, so budgets MULTIPLY: m pieces give m*d. Check the count uses every number given; a lone d or m dropped a factor.

Attain it with consecutive blocks, one piece each.
hints.mutation: lead with a do-not-invent-constraints rule (reuse allowed unless forbidden; a whole-pattern condition need not hold piecewise) and an exit for impossible/unbounded branches, plus an agreement-count framing that pins the per-piece cap at the stated degree

Two more applied the multiplied budget correctly in form but with a per-piece cap one below the degree stated in the problem, having subtracted the affine target and then differenced again. So the incumbent needs less residual bookkeeping and more license discipline: state up front that reuse is permitted unless forbidden and that a whole-pattern condition need not hold piece by piece, give impossible/unbounded branches a one-line exit, and pin the per-piece cap by counting agreements with the line at the degree exactly as given.

hints.hint: Name your unknowns and turn each given condition into one exact equation; solve for any constants first. Reduce to a single variable, keep exact fractions, and discard roots that are degenerate or outside the domain. Verify a candidate by substituting it back into the original conditions, not by re-deriving; once it passes, stop revisiting it. Re-read the question and report the exact quantity it asks for, simplified. State your result early, then stop.
hints.mutation: swap the costly second-method verification for substitute-back checking, a no-re-verify stop, and a re-read-the-question step

hints.hint:
Randomness over STEPS is not uniformity over OUTCOMES. "Random permutation", 1/n, k!/n! are guesses: many step sequences collapse to one ordering, and some orderings are unreachable.

Orientation is mechanical, not a choice. Items land on TOP, so a pile bottom is its EARLIEST arrival, never the one moved last. An intermediate pile also releases its top first, so an item leaves it only after everything that entered later has left. Label the start pile bottom-to-top before naming the asked item.

Those facts convert "this item arrives first" into an exact opening block of loads before the first unload. That prefix decides the event; later steps cannot.

Now LIST the prefix steps: 1/2 only where both moves are legal, 1 where a side is empty or exhausted; report 2^(-free steps listed). Never overwrite a value you listed steps for with a symmetry story; drop the unlisted rival and stop.
hints.mutation: make orientation mechanical (label the source pile, buffer releases top first) so the asked slot becomes an exact opening load block, and forbid overwriting a step-listed value with an unlisted symmetry claim
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling gave 2/8; seven rollouts stopped normally and one hit the cap relitigating, so length is secondary. Part (a) is mostly solved (five reached the free-step count), and every loss was the slot part: six asserted a uniform random permutation and read off 1/n or 3!/4!, each having first equated the deepest slot with 'moved last'. Two rollouts even derived the correct free-step value and then explicitly overwrote it with a symmetry story a paragraph later. Several also mislabelled the start pile orientation, so they named the wrong item. The revision makes orientation mechanical rather than a reading to pick, adds the buffer rule that an item leaves only after later entrants, converts the slot event into an exact opening block of loads, and forbids overwriting a step-listed value with an unlisted symmetry claim.

hints.hint: Translate the setup once and never restate it: re-describing the given conditions in fresh notation is the biggest waste of budget, and an unlanded derivation scores nothing. At a large or symbolic size, get a number on the page fast -- solve the smallest honest instance exactly, write its value down, and never re-derive a case you already settled. Extend to a second and third instance; two entries only hint at a form, while three separate factorials from powers from alternating signs. Read entries by ratio as well as difference, and track sign apart from size. Treat your own hesitation as a deadline: the moment you catch yourself stuck, or asking how to proceed, or opening yet another approach, stop exploring, commit the result your confirmed entries best support, and spend what remains testing it against them rather than hunting a general proof.
hints.mutation: turn self-reported stalling into an explicit stop-and-commit trigger; ban restating the setup; require a third instance to distinguish growth types
hints.subagent_summary: All eight fresh rollouts hit the generation cap and none emitted a result, so this round scored zero purely on budget exhaustion, not on reasoning ability. Every transcript spent its opening paragraphs re-paraphrasing the given conditions in new notation, then cycled through abstract framings, and several literally wrote that they were stuck or out of ideas and opened yet another approach instead of landing anything. Some had already computed correct small instances and still never committed. The incumbent asks for early commitment but gives no trigger for it, so the revision bans restating the setup, demands a written value from the smallest instance immediately, requires a third instance to separate factorial from power growth, and converts the model own stuck/how-do-I-proceed language into an explicit stop-and-commit deadline.

hints.hint: Let H be the total number of houses. The equal-street layout constrains H arithmetically, and integer stage costs per house mean H must divide every listed stage total. Determine the admissible common divisors using the intended maximum-feasible-count interpretation. Add all construction costs before dividing by H, and apply the stated markup multiplicatively. In general, when a direct attack stalls, work the smallest cases by hand and read off the pattern or invariant rather than pushing a long computation. Treat every value you derive as a candidate and screen it: reject any that breaks a stated restriction such as positivity, integrality, or a range limit, and re-test roots created by squaring or clearing denominators. Check that every given number was used; an unused given signals a misread. State your result plainly as soon as you have it.
hints.mutation: keep the train-safe opening and small-cases clause verbatim; replace the never-exercised exact-fractions clause with an untried candidate-screening rule (reject values violating positivity/integrality/range, re-test extraneous roots) plus an all-givens-used misread check

What the rollouts do spend real effort on is enumerating divisor candidates and then arguing which survive the stated conditions, and they only converge after discarding the ones that conflict with a given. I generalized exactly that observed move into a reusable candidate-screening rule covering positivity, integrality, range limits and extraneous roots from squaring or clearing denominators, and added an all-givens-used check since misreads are the residual failure class. Screening and extraneous-root discipline are untried in prior rounds here.

hints.hint: Never name unknown coefficients and never expand a composed or high-degree identity; that exhausts your budget. Recenter about one shared unknown center c: f=c+a(x-c)^k, g=c-a(x-c)^k, odd k, opposite signs, no offset, so the identity collapses by symmetry. The supplied values are then c-a*c^k and c+a*c^k: adding cancels the a-term and pins c linearly; subtracting isolates a. An irrational center is a sign slip; fix that line, never expand. An input equal to c or a fixed point is immediate. Read requested values off that centered form, never a re-expanded standard-power version, which re-adds the constant the center already carries. A value that already matched the given data is settled: a disagreeing rewrite is the error, not the value. Record each requested value at once and stop.
hints.mutation: forbid re-expansion into standard powers when reading off results and add a settled-value rule (a checked value outranks a later disagreeing rewrite), replacing the redundant same-sign/factor-out warnings
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling gave 3/8 correct, down from the incumbent's earlier 8/8, and the failures split cleanly. Four rollouts never adopted the centered form and burned all 16384 tokens matching coefficients of the degree-9 composition, chasing sign contradictions in their own expansions. The one rollout that terminated wrong had already recentered, pinned the center and scale correctly, and verified both supplied values, then re-expanded into standard powers, wrongly re-added the given constant on top of the center, distrusted its verified values, and overwrote them with the corrupted ones. The revision therefore keeps the recentering core but spends its tokens on the two live traps: evaluate only inside the centered form, and treat a value that already matched the data as settled so a later disagreeing rewrite is discarded instead of the value.

hints.hint: Let the requested form of the result police your work: a result that must be an expression in a parameter has to move with that parameter, so a case coming out constant is mis-traced. Repair it before fitting, and require your formula to reproduce every case you trust, including the smallest. Get cases cheaply and concretely: run the stated procedure literally on one small instance, each step acting on the previous step's output, never on the original data. Then obey a stopping rule. Once a candidate matches every case you traced, you are done; you do not owe a general proof, and abandoning agreeing cases to redo the work symbolically is how these attempts die. Treat repetition as an exit signal, not a puzzle: if you catch yourself rewriting the same expression, calling the setup confusing, or reaching for yet another approach, stop there and state the value your cases support.
hints.mutation: add an explicit sufficiency/stopping rule (agreeing cases are enough, no general proof owed) and make self-repetition or confusion a hard exit signal rather than a cue to restart symbolically
hints.subagent_summary: 5 of 8 rollouts were correct and every one read the pattern straight off two or three literal small traces, then stopped. All 3 failures ran to the 16384-token cap, and none failed for lack of a correct case: each had already produced small-case values matching the eventual pattern, then discarded them as 'tedious' and switched to a symbolic product-of-permutations derivation. Two degenerated into verbatim repetition loops of one cycle expression; one drifted into a bogus larger count and hunted an unrelated integer sequence. So the binding constraint is no longer how cases get traced, since the incumbent's clause already works, but the absence of permission to stop once cases agree. The revision keeps the parameter-shape check and literal tracing, adds an explicit sufficiency rule (agreeing cases mean done, no general proof owed), and makes self-repetition or 'confusing' a hard exit.
